utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the Registrar call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-00-39 & 40-PT, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik and Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours. Alan Tieger on behalf of the prosecution appearing with Mr. Fergal Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Deyan Brashich for the Krajisnik Defence. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The application today that the Trial Chamber is dealing with is an application for provisional release by Mr. Krajisnik. We have in front of us the motion and response, we have a number of guarantees from Republika Srpska, we have an undertaking from Mr. Krajisnik himself, an undertaking from Mr. Brashich, and we also have statements from the patriarch and from Mr. Kostunica. Now, Mr. Brashich, is it right that there is a representative of the government here today?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is. The only other thing which was filed just last night is two addendums. One is a guarantee from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the second addendum is a statement that, if necessary, the Republic of Serbia will add its own guarantee, even though it is a constituent part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The only other assurances that is also before the Court is that I have been authorised by the immediate members of Mr. Krajisnik's family that real property and improvements, both within the Federation and the Republic of Srpska would -- deeds to those real properties and improvements, deeds to those properties, would be signed in blank and lodged with the registrar and would be forfeited in the event that Mr. Krajisnik does not fulfil the terms and conditions of his provisional release or return back to the Tribunal for trial. In effect, the family would be homeless and without a roof over their heads should Mr. Krajisnik not return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, I wonder if it might be of assistance if we now read the motion which you -- the addendum which you put in, together with the guarantee.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would sit down, we'll read that and then we will hear your submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've read that. Mr. Brashich, now, what would you like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Krajisnik Defence urges provisional release for Mr. Krajisnik. I think certain factors weigh in the favour of provisional release. Mr. Krajisnik was not aware of the sealed indictment. Had he known, he would have volunteered and surrendered voluntarily. Mr. Krajisnik has been incarcerated for approximately a year and a half. Mr. Krajisnik is willing to be provisionally released, should the Court favour the request, either in the Republic of Srpska or in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, specifically in Belgrade, where his brother resides and has an apartment. Mr. Krajisnik has, in the past, cooperated with the Tribunal, and Mr. Krajisnik met, when he was the President of the Assembly, or the Parliament, with Madam Arbour. At the present time, it is at the direction of his attorney, myself, that he is not cooperating because of the pending indictment. The Republika Srpska - and its representative is here to address the Court - is in the process of changing its stance with regard to cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, could you explain what you meant when you said that in the past, he had cooperated with the Tribunal, with the former Prosecutor, Madam Arbour. What was the extent of that cooperation?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: He met with her, Your Honour, and thereafter he met with members of her staff and gave an extensive interview, which was taped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That was the extent of the cooperation?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's all that was asked of him. In his position as the President of the Assembly, he had no executive power subsequent to the Dayton Accord. And with leave of the Court, I should like at this time to ask whether or not Mr. Sinisa Djordjevic, a representative of the President, Mr. Ivanic, could address the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Should he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. From counsel's bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours of the Trial Chamber, dear colleagues, my name is Sinisa Djordjevic. I am the adviser of the President -- Prime Minister of the Republika Srpska for relations with the Tribunal in The Hague. I am a lawyer by profession. I have come before you here today, your distinguished excellencies and my learned colleagues, to convey to you the position of the government of Republika Srpska with respect to the request made by Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik for provisional release until the beginning of his trial. I have been authorised to convey the fact that the Prime Minister, Mr. Ivanic, adheres fully to the statement he gave on the 27th of August this year, and the component part of that statement is a special guarantee issued by the government of Republika Srpska, which you yourselves have already received, so there is no need for me to expound it further. Furthermore, the government of Republika Srpska, which I represent here, is well-apprised of the fact that there is a conclusion made by this august Tribunal with respect to the fact that Republika Srpska was not sufficiently cooperative -- was not sufficiently disposed to cooperate with The Hague Tribunal. I should like to ask you that you take my position with respect to the government that I represent today and assess it in those terms. It is -- the fact is exact that the governments hitherto of Republika Srpska were indeed not sufficiently cooperative with The Hague Tribunal. However, I should like now, if I may, to say a few words about that, to say what the new government has in fact done in relation to The Hague Tribunal. Whether it is sufficient or not, you yourselves will assess. First and foremost, on the 23rd of March this year, a commission was set up, or rather a department attached to the Justice Ministry of Republika Srpska, for relations with The Hague Tribunal. The department, seven days ago, grew to become a bureau, a full-fledged bureau of Republika Srpska for its relations with The Hague Tribunal as a specialised body which in future will not be dependent upon changes and vagaries in politics and policies of other structures in Republika Srpska, depending on the change of government and authority. We are also well aware of the fact that this government has put forward a draft for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Before you continue, would you just explain what is the precise function of this new bureau which you say has been set up and apparently, from what you say, has a measure of independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. Let me explain the difference. First of all, it was a fact that depending on the change in government structures, there was a change in the individuals and their way of thinking with respect to the country's relationship towards the Tribunal. It was our idea to set up this special body and organ Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which, for the moment and temporarily, and I emphasise only temporarily as attached to the Justice Ministry of Republika Srpska, but that it should take on a new function, especially in view of the fact that it will be composed of a team of experts, of individuals who are not politically oriented and tinged, so that they would be able to prevent, depending on their own political interests, any relationships with the Tribunal. They would not be able to do that any longer. Do you wish me to say anything else? Does that satisfy you, Your Honour? Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but I still am not clear as to what this bureau is supposed to do. You have told me about its members, but what is it designed to do in its relationship with the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This bureau was established by the bill and law for cooperation with the Tribunal in The Hague, and it is expected to be adopted today, and at the latest tomorrow, in fact. The draft law envisages that it is the Bureau which is to be the protagonist of cooperation with the Tribunal, and this in practical terms means that in future, all contacts and requests made by the Tribunal, its demands, will pass through a filter, which is the Bureau. The Bureau of Republika Srpska will be this filter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Furthermore, as far as the activities of Republika Srpska itself is concerned, you are well aware of the fact that this present government, whose representative I am myself and which issues guarantees for Mr. Krajisnik today, has put on its agenda finally the law on cooperation with the International Tribunal in The Hague. I think -- let me also say the following: Regardless of whether justified or not justified reasons which speak of the fact whether this law is necessary or not, we consider that this particular law or act or bill will have full legal force and we give it priority importance. We give priority and importance to cooperation with the Tribunal, and with the enactment of this law, we are duty-bound to fulfil this relationship of cooperation with the Tribunal. In this regard, and in conclusion, let me say the following: I should like to convey the apologies of Mr. Mladen Ivancic, the prime minister of Republika Srpska - Ivanic, I'm sorry - who personally signed the guarantee on behalf of the government, and I should like to explain why he has not been able to attend this august Tribunal. The reason is that the premier today in the Assembly of Republika Srpska, as the authorised person to put forward the law on cooperation with the Tribunal, is duty-bound to be there and to see if there are any different opinions, but his job is to achieve our goal and aim, together with the other Assembly members, and that is to ensure that the bill is turned into a law today or tomorrow. Thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic. You may take it that as far as the prime minister is concerned, we accept, of course, that there was no discourtesy intended by the fact that he is not here, and you are well able to represent him. Yes, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic has just handed me the originals of the guarantee and his power of attorney, which I will lodge thereafter. Your Honour, I think I've said everything that I can on behalf of my client. We have seen that three individuals who have been given provisional release have returned to the seat of the Tribunal. We have seen an evolvement of the way that the Republika Srpska perceives of this Court. We also have seen that Mrs. Plavsic has returned to Belgrade. The only other assurance that I want to give to the Chamber, and perhaps this should come from Mr. Krajisnik's own lips, is that he has respect for the Tribunal, he will respect the terms and conditions, and that he has a host of reasons why it is imperative for him to return for trial. Should he fail to do so, he would have violated the trust that the patriarch had in him; he would become a pariah within his own people. Should he not return, he would have violated the trust of President Kostunica and his government. Should he fail to return, he would not be able to vindicate his name and his actions during the period of time when he was in government. Should he fail to return, he would have violated his own family and rendered them homeless. Should he fail to return, he would have violated his word to this Court and again would make him a pariah within his own people. I'm not as eloquent as Mr. Krajisnik was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: There was another thing that Mr. Krajisnik told me yesterday afternoon. I had placed my word, should he breach that word, that promise to return, and the conditions of his provisional release, no other attorney would represent him. I am not as eloquent as Mr. Krajisnik was yesterday afternoon, and I don't know whether the Court would wish to hear from Mr. Krajisnik's own lips his assurances and warranties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Brashich, you put it very fully. We've heard your submissions. You've put them fully before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Then I rest. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger? When you're addressing this question, would you have in mind, in particular, the amount of time which this accused has been in custody, and the possible date for trial, which is a matter of concern, of course, to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Let me begin with the simple legal --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let me begin by noting that it is the accused's burden to establish that the conditions necessary for granting of this motion are satisfied, and it is a substantial burden indeed. There may come a time when the guarantees of Republika Srpska and the other assurances offered by the Defence are sufficient to constitute a significant factor in the Court's consideration of whether that burden has been discharged, but it is clear that that date has not yet arrived. We have heard repeatedly about draft legislation, about actions that will be undertaken in the future. In this particular case, we are dealing with legislation that has not been passed to establish a bureau, the effectiveness of which we have no way of knowing about. In light of that, all we can look to is the history of cooperation and apprehension to determine whether or not those guarantees have value. And the Court has already made a determination, as have other Chambers, about the weight that can be given to that history and about the implications of that. Let me also speak briefly to some of the other assurances that were offered by the accused. Mr. Brashich made reference to the declarations of Patriarch Pavle and to the declarations of Mr. Kostunica. I note in that regard that the patriarch was a signatory to a declaration that asserted that the indictment of Mr. Karadzic and the consequent pressure by the international community for his apprehension were illegitimate and had nothing to do with international law. I noted in Mr. Kostunica's declaration that he, among other things, offered, in effect, a character reference for Mr. Krajisnik, asserting that, based on his dealings with Mr. Krajisnik, he was satisfied that he was a man of integrity and his word could be trusted. First of all, I note that the context in which that impression was formed is surely different from one in which the accused faces a substantial period of incarceration, a substantial risk of incarceration, when being tried by an institution which he has previously asserted lacked partiality. I think those are factors that militate strongly against willing submission to this institution's authority. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Furthermore, I noted that Mr. Kostunica referred to the, quote, "brutal" apprehension of Mr. Krajisnik, a characterisation that I found, at a minimum, insensitive in the context in the war in former Yugoslavia and the charges which this accused faces. I also noted that it was not the first time that such reference was made by Mr. Kostunica, who referred previously to the brutal arrest and went on to say, as quoted, "It is crystal clear that the War Crimes Tribunal is neither a legal, nor a judicial, nor an international institution." He went on to say it is merely a tool and to characterise it as being a weapon in a war against Serbs. I think those -- reliance on such references is also a matter of some significance to the Court. I further noted that Mr. Kostunica promoted the notion of Mr. Krajisnik's release as having beneficial impact on relationships between this institution and the Bosnian Serbs, a factor which I would suggest, if relevant, is dramatically outweighed by the adverse impact on the millions of victims of the crimes committed during this war, on the victims who risked their lives by coming to testify before this institution, and on the SFOR personnel who risk their lives in efforts to apprehend outstanding suspects. Mr. Djordjevic correctly noted in his introductory remarks that the Court previously determined that the history of cooperation by Republika Srpska was insufficient to satisfy the Court that it could rely that the accused would be apprehended if he fled. Today, in contrast to the situation when the Court made that determination, the risks of flight by the accused are exponentially greater because of the length of time involved between now and trial, in contrast to the motion that was previously made, and the assurances, the safeguards, that can be offered are correspondingly less. For that reason, Your Honours, the Prosecution vigorously opposes this motion and submits that it should be denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you haven't dealt -- we'll hear you in a moment, Mr. Brashich. You haven't dealt with the matter I raised, which is this: You refer to the length of time between now and trial. Eighteen months this accused has been in custody already. Now, that is a matter of concern to any Tribunal, any judicial body. He's in custody and he hasn't been tried. And it's a factor we are going to have to consider. When do you anticipate this case will be ready for trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understood from the Court that the matter was set for trial in February. I understand that to be the current date. Let me -- I apologise for not addressing the point the Court raised earlier. The question of the length of detention has been addressed in international law in various contexts. It has been found, as I understand it, to be related to the complexity and magnitude and gravity of the case. In circumstances -- in cases involving circumstances far less complex - because this is indeed, as the Court is aware, a case of unusual complexity - and of lesser magnitude, to be certain, the period of acceptable pre-trial detention has ranged from 19 months to five years, and that is contained in a previous submission by the Prosecution. Certainly no one can be happy with any period of pre-trial detention, but sometimes it is a necessary concomitant of the case, and that is the fact here. In addition, we have been moving, as the Court is aware, as vigorously as possible toward getting this matter to trial, and the Court has been pushing that as effectively as it can, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Prosecution, then, will be ready for trial in February?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I stated before during our Status Conference, we have had that in mind since the Court first raised that date. We are doing everything humanly possible to make that date. That is the date we have in mind, based on what the Court has told us. That is what we are working toward, and we are doing everything possible to satisfy that objective by the Court and by us as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would you like to comment on the offer of guarantees from the Republic of Serbia in terms identical to those which were offered and accepted by this Chamber in respect of Mrs. Plavsic? In relation to Mrs. Plavsic, a significant factor was the fact of her voluntary surrender. In that regard, perhaps you'd like to comment on the submission from the Defence that, in the case of Mr. Krajisnik, there was a sealed indictment, of which he was not aware, and that that was a significant factor explaining why he did not surrender voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You raise several questions. Let me take them serially. First of all, with respect to the question of Mr. Krajisnik's apprehension, the Prosecution has never attempted to assert or to characterise that apprehension as equivalent to flight. What is true, however, is that Mrs. Plavsic did voluntarily surrender. That was a factor that could be considered positively by this Chamber, and was. That factor is not available to Mr. Krajisnik, for circumstances that have been outlined. We are not attempting to transform this into a negative factor; however, we reject any attempt by the Defence to transform it into a positive factor. It is not. That positive factor existed for Mrs. Plavsic. It does not here. Insofar as the guarantees are concerned, Your Honour, I just received them approximately five minutes before the hearing began. I read them, as Your Honours did, in the course of this proceeding. I'm slightly hesitant to comment on the precise nature of those guarantees, based on a superficial reading. However, I should point out that my understanding is that the guarantees in front of the Court today come from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Mrs. Plavsic's guarantees came from the Republic of Serbia. The question of whose authorities, whose hands-on authorities would be responsible, is one which is raised by that distinction. In addition, I am advised that during the Prosecutor's last visit to Belgrade, she was informed by federal authorities that they had not passed draft legislation in connection with cooperation with the Tribunal, and until such time as such legislation was passed, they would be unable to offer assurances that arrests would be effected. So although I have not had a full opportunity to either study these personally or have them reviewed by people with greater expertise in the area than I possess, it appears to me that they are not the same assurances that this Court relied on in making a determination within Mrs. Plavsic's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will check that, Mr. Tieger. We can compare the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may make one final point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that is, I think these matters must be determined on a case-by-case basis. I know I'm not telling the Court anything new in saying that, but I mention that because Mrs. Plavsic's situation does not necessarily lend itself to a simple checklist of similarities. There were a variety of subjective factors and subtle nuanced factors that led the Prosecution to withdraw opposition to her release in that case. And although I can't recite the precise history and all the circumstances that led to that, I think the Court was aware of those as the case progressed, to some extent relied on the Prosecution to make its determination based on the many factors known to it and the information available to it, which could not possibly be recited in a single court hearing, and that was the basis for the Prosecution's position in that case. And I think the Chamber needs to keep in mind the variety of circumstances which can lead a court to find that the substantial burden by the Defence has been met in its application for provisional release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brashich.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly. The February date, while this has been discussed at Status Conferences, we're still getting Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. documents and translations. We still haven't got all of them. I don't see February as a feasible trial date. We have filed -- the Defence has filed jointly a response to the conditional pre-trial brief, so I do not believe that February is a realistic date. Two, I do not see the difference and the nuances that the Prosecution sees between Mr. Krajisnik and Mrs. Plavsic. Mrs. Plavsic enjoyed a far greater role in the government of the Republika Srpska than did Mr. Krajisnik. I don't believe that your question, Judge Robinson, was answered by Mr. Tieger. Just a moment, Your Honour. And, of course, the presumption of innocence has attached to Mr. Krajisnik. Finally, the positions taken by politicians in pronouncements are one thing; reflections upon a person's character are a totally different thing. Mr. Krajisnik is not to be tarred by any opinion that Mr. Krajisnik may have had. Finally, the arrest of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: As that reads, you say the opinion Mr. Krajisnik may have held?

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: Well, the opinion that Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I see what you mean. You're saying the fact that he may have held an opinion does not affect his character. That's the point. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRASHICH
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honour, if you recall, there was all that correspondence between SFOR and my client prior to his arrest and then his arrest. One wonders, why was Mrs. Plavsic told that there was an indictment while Mr. Krajisnik was not? And why was Mrs. Plavsic told eight months later after the indictment had been filed that she was an accused, and not my client? Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. If I can briefly respond to those comments. Number one, it is not the Prosecution's position that Mr. Krajisnik's position in government was far less than Mrs. Plavsic's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's really just a matter for argument at trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but to the extent that counsel raised it, I didn't want that to go unanswered. Number two - and again, I don't want to belabour this. I'm sure the Court knows it - the presumption of innocence has a significant role in a proceeding. Its invocation here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you needn't address us on those points.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider these matters, and we will give a decision in writing. The Court will adjourn.
